NSAIDs, Acetaminophen, DMARDs, and Drugs for Gout

Explanation-focused interactive reviewer based only on the uploaded lecture

0
Orientation

See the whole lesson before learning the parts

This lecture moves from the inflammatory pathway to symptom control, then to urate lowering and disease modification. The central task is choosing the right drug for the right therapeutic goal while respecting the major toxicities and exceptions.

01Inflammation

Identify the protective response and the two therapeutic goals.

02COX and NSAIDs

Connect prostanoid inhibition to analgesic, antipyretic, anti-inflammatory, gastric, renal, and platelet effects.

03Pain control

Distinguish NSAIDs from paracetamol, ketorolac, and tramadol.

04Gout

Separate acute anti-inflammatory treatment from chronic urate-lowering therapy.

05Rheumatoid arthritis

Use DMARDs to slow tissue damage, then understand major synthetic and biologic targets.

Central question

Which process is the drug changing? Some drugs suppress prostanoids, some lower urate, and some suppress immune pathways that drive rheumatoid arthritis.

Highest-yield distinction

NSAIDs relieve symptoms but do not alter the course of arthritis. DMARDs can slow the tissue-damaging process in rheumatic disease. pp. 3, 9

Organizing rule

Acute problems need rapid control. Chronic gout needs urate lowering. Rheumatoid arthritis needs disease modification.

High-yield orientation table
Clinical goalMain drug groups in the lectureWhat the learner should track
Reduce fever, pain, and inflammationNSAIDs, paracetamol, ketorolac, tramadolCOX selectivity, platelet effect, GI risk, CV risk, renal risk, and liver toxicity
Relieve acute goutNSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoids, selected IL-1 inhibitorsInflammatory-cell migration, prostaglandins, IL-1, contraindications, and timing
Lower urate chronicallyAllopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid, pegloticaseProduction versus excretion, flare prophylaxis, hypersensitivity, CV warning, stones, and G6PD deficiency
Slow rheumatoid arthritisConventional synthetic, targeted synthetic, biologic, and biosimilar DMARDsImmune target, infection risk, organ toxicity, route, and combination strategy

Must-know exceptions

  • Nabumetone is the only non-acid NSAID. p. 4
  • Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX. Other NSAIDs inhibit reversibly. p. 3
  • Selective COX-2 inhibitors and non-acetylated salicylates do not inhibit platelet aggregation. p. 2
  • Aspirin, salicylates, and tolmetin are not used successfully for acute gout in the lecture. pp. 5, 7
  • Indomethacin or ibuprofen can be used to close a patent ductus arteriosus in preterm infants. p. 4

Major antidotes and rescue measures

  • Aspirin poisoning → IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize urine and enhance elimination
  • Paracetamol poisoning → N-acetylcysteine to help neutralize NAPQI
  • Methotrexate toxicity → leucovorin or folic acid reduces selected adverse effects
  • Leflunomide → cholestyramine shortens the prolonged half-life
  • Cyclophosphamide → hydration and mesna address acrolein-related bladder toxicity
pp. 3, 5, 10, 11, 14

How the topics connect

Inflammation explains NSAID action. The COX pathway explains both therapeutic effects and toxicities. Gout then shows why the same anti-inflammatory drugs can treat an acute flare without correcting urate burden. Rheumatoid arthritis completes the lesson by introducing drugs that modify the underlying disease process.

Foundation

Inflammation and the COX pathway

Start with the protective response, then follow arachidonic acid toward prostanoids. This pathway explains why NSAIDs reduce fever, pain, and inflammation.

What inflammation is

Inflammation is the response of vascularized tissues to infection and tissue damage. It brings host-defense cells and molecules from the circulation to the site where they are needed. Without it, infections could go unchecked, wounds would not heal, and damaged tissue could persist. p. 1

Five cardinal signs

Heat

Redness

Swelling

Pain

Loss of function

When the response becomes the problem

  • Autoimmune disease redirects inflammation against self, as in rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Allergy directs inflammation against harmless environmental substances.
  • Inadequate control allows inflammation to continue beyond its protective purpose.

Two therapeutic goals

  1. Relieve symptoms and maintain function. Reduce pain and other inflammatory signs so function can be restored.
  2. Slow or arrest tissue damage. This is especially important in chronic disease and is achieved by DMARDs in rheumatic disease.
pp. 1, 9

COX isoenzymes

  • COX-1 produces prostanoids for housekeeping functions, including gastric epithelial cytoprotection.
  • COX-2 is a major source of inflammation and cancer.
  • Endothelial COX-2 is a primary source of prostacyclin.
  • Renal COX-2 is important for normal renal development.
p. 2

How COX inhibition relieves fever, pain, and inflammation

1. Arachidonic acidProvides substrate for cyclooxygenase.
2. COX-2 activityProduces prostanoids involved in fever, pain, and inflammation.
3. NSAID inhibitionReduces prostanoid biosynthesis.
4. Downstream effectLower PGE2 reduces body temperature. Lower PGE2 and PGI2 reduce pain and inflammation.

What this flow means: NSAIDs act chiefly by reducing prostanoids. The lecture also lists possible additional effects on chemotaxis, IL-1 production, free radicals, superoxide, and calcium-mediated intracellular events. pp. 1–2

Lock It In

  • Core concept: inflammation is protective until it becomes misdirected or inadequately controlled.
  • Key differentiator: COX-1 supports housekeeping functions while COX-2 is a major inflammatory source.
  • Key sequence: arachidonic acid → COX → prostanoids → fever, pain, inflammation, platelet, gastric, and vascular effects.
  • Exam cue: reducing PGE2 lowers body temperature.
Core pharmacology

What all NSAIDs share and where selectivity changes the outcome

NSAIDs are united by prostanoid inhibition, but their effects on COX-1 and COX-2 determine gastric and cardiovascular tradeoffs.

Common chemistry and pharmacokinetics

  • Weak organic acids: all NSAIDs except nabumetone.
  • Nabumetone: a ketone prodrug that becomes an acidic active drug.
  • Absorption: generally well absorbed. Food does not substantially change bioavailability.
  • Distribution: about 98 percent protein bound, usually to albumin. Repeated dosing places drug in synovial fluid.
  • Metabolism: extensive hepatic metabolism through phase I, phase II, direct glucuronidation, or CYP3A and CYP2C pathways.
  • Excretion: renal elimination is most important. Biliary excretion and enterohepatic recirculation may occur.
p. 1

Four therapeutic effects

Analgesic

Reduces pain.

Anti-inflammatory

Reduces prostanoid-mediated inflammation.

Antipyretic

Reduces fever through lower PGE2.

Antiplatelet

Usually reversible, except aspirin. Selective COX-2 inhibitors and non-acetylated salicylates are exceptions.

p. 2
Non-selective COX inhibitors versus selective COX-2 inhibitors
FeatureNon-selective COX inhibitionSelective COX-2 inhibition
Inflammation controlReduces COX-2 prostanoidsReduces COX-2 prostanoids
Gastric protectionCOX-1 inhibition reduces PGE-mediated cytoprotectionCOX-1 is preserved, so GI irritation is lower
Platelet balanceReduces platelet thromboxane and endothelial prostacyclin. Net effect inhibits platelet aggregationReduces prostacyclin without blocking platelet thromboxane
Clinical emphasisRelatively safer for patients with cardiovascular disease in the lectureRelatively safer for GERD, but not cardioprotective
Shared pointThe lecture states that both groups are equally efficacious and carry black-box warnings.

Major toxicity pattern

  • Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain, dyspepsia, nausea, vomiting, ulcers, and bleeding
  • Cardiovascular: fluid retention, hypertension, myocardial infarction, and heart failure
  • Renal: insufficiency, failure, hyperkalemia, and proteinuria
  • Hepatic: abnormal liver tests and rare liver failure
  • Other: headache, tinnitus, dizziness, asthma, rashes, pruritus, and rare hematologic effects
p. 3

Black-box and pregnancy warnings

  • Cardiovascular: serious thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke may be fatal. Risk increases with longer use and pre-existing risk.
  • Gastrointestinal: bleeding, ulceration, and perforation may occur without warning. Older patients are at greater risk.
  • Pregnancy at 20 weeks or later: risk of low amniotic fluid.
  • Pregnancy at 30 weeks or later: risk of premature closure of the fetal ductus arteriosus.
p. 3

Lock It In

  • Core concept: all NSAIDs chiefly inhibit prostanoid biosynthesis.
  • Key differentiator: COX-1 inhibition increases GI injury but reduces platelet aggregation.
  • Key sequence: COX-2 block → lower inflammation and pain. Prostacyclin block without thromboxane block → thrombosis risk.
  • Exam cue: use the lowest effective dose for the shortest possible treatment period.
Drug families

NSAID agents and the exceptions that make them testable

The lecture emphasizes aspirin, selected non-selective agents, and coxibs. Focus on irreversible action, organ toxicity, and special indications.

Aspirin

  • Also called: acetylsalicylic acid
  • Antiplatelet dose: 80 to 325 mg once daily
  • Mechanism: irreversible COX inhibition. Platelet effect lasts for the platelet lifespan, about 8 to 10 days in the lecture.
  • Low doses: preferential COX-1 inhibition
  • Higher doses: systemic COX-1 and COX-2 inhibition
  • Urine alkalinization: IV sodium bicarbonate raises urine pH and increases excretion in poisoning.
  • Clinical uses listed: reduces coronary thrombosis with myocardial infarction, bypass graft thrombosis, transient ischemic attacks, and unstable angina.
p. 3

Aspirin safety traps

  • Do not use for gout analgesia. At doses at or below 2.6 g per day, aspirin causes renal uric acid retention.
  • Reye syndrome: avoid aspirin for fever in children with influenza or varicella.
  • Major adverse effects: gastric upset, gastric and duodenal ulcers, GI bleeding, asthma, rash, hepatotoxicity, and renal toxicity.
  • Before elective surgery: the lecture uses one week as the discontinuation interval when the risk-benefit analysis supports stopping.
  • Dual antiplatelet therapy: aspirin plus clopidogrel reduces cardiovascular events more than aspirin alone but increases major bleeding.
pp. 3–4

Lock It In

  • Core concept: agent selection depends more on safety and patient factors than efficacy because the lecture states that NSAIDs are equally efficacious.
  • Key differentiator: aspirin is irreversible.
  • Key sequence: aspirin at analgesic doses → uric acid retention → avoid in gout.
  • Exam cue: ketorolac is an NSAID used for analgesia only and for no more than five days.
Patient-centered choice

ESSC, paracetamol, ketorolac, tramadol, and the analgesic ladder

When efficacy is similar, the best choice depends on safety, suitability, and cost. The other analgesics then separate pain relief from anti-inflammatory action.

ESSC framework

  • Efficacy: all NSAIDs are equally efficacious in the lecture, with practical exceptions such as tolmetin for gout.
  • Safety: match GI, CV, renal, hepatic, and hematologic risks to the patient.
  • Suitability: consider other medicines, allergies, comorbidities, formulation, dosing schedule, and adherence.
  • Cost-effectiveness: there is no single best NSAID for every patient.
p. 5

Choice patterns from the lecture

  • Renal insufficiency: non-acetylated salicylates
  • High GI bleeding risk: celecoxib or low-dose non-selective NSAID plus omeprazole
  • High CV disease risk: non-selective NSAID
  • Toxicity survey: indomethacin and tolmetin are most toxic. Salsalate, aspirin, and ibuprofen are least toxic.
p. 5

Paracetamol or acetaminophen

Paracetamol is a weak COX-1 and COX-2 inhibitor in peripheral tissues. It provides analgesia and antipyresis but has no significant anti-inflammatory effect. It does not affect platelet function or uric acid levels. p. 5

Uses and dosing in the lecture

  • Acute pain and fever: 10 to 15 mg per kg per dose in children. Adults receive 325 to 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, with a listed maximum of 4 g per day.
  • Mild to moderate pain: headache, myalgia, and postpartum pain.
  • Preferred to aspirin: in aspirin allergy or intolerance, hemophilia, peptic ulcer history, aspirin-triggered bronchospasm, and children with fever.

Pharmacokinetics

  • Peak plasma: 30 to 60 minutes after oral dosing
  • Protein binding: poor
  • Metabolism: mainly inactive sulfate and glucuronide metabolites
  • Half-life: 2 to 3 hours, at least doubled in liver disease

Paracetamol hepatotoxicity

  • Major toxicity: liver injury
  • Potential toxicity: 7 g per day in adults and 150 to 200 mg per kg in children
  • Potentially fatal dose: 15 g per day in the lecture
  • Early symptoms: diarrhea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and nausea
  • Progression: hepatic encephalopathy and renal failure may follow severe hepatic impairment
  • Antidote: N-acetylcysteine as early as possible
  • Liver disease, malnutrition, and alcoholism: the lecture advises dose reduction or avoidance because usual pathways fall and CYP450 metabolism is induced.
pp. 5–6

Ketorolac

  • Role: analgesic NSAID with poor anti-inflammatory usefulness in the lecture
  • Duration: no more than five days
  • Use: moderate to severe pain and postoperative pain, often with another analgesic or anesthetic
  • Routes: IV, IM, intranasal, oral, and ophthalmic
  • Elimination: about 90 percent renal, with about 60 percent unchanged
  • Dose reduction: halve doses in age over 65 years, body weight below 50 kg, or renal impairment
  • Main concern: nephrotoxicity, especially with chronic use
p. 6

Tramadol

  • Class: weak opioid or miscellaneous opioid analgesic
  • Mechanism: weak μ-opioid receptor affinity plus inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake
  • Naloxone: blocks only about 30 percent of the analgesic effect in the lecture
  • No significant anti-inflammatory action
  • Common effects: nausea, vomiting, vertigo, dizziness, tiredness, sedation, dry mouth, constipation, and sweating
  • Serious concerns: serotonin syndrome with antidepressants and seizures in susceptible patients
p. 6

Three-step pain ladder

  1. Step 1: non-opioids such as NSAIDs and paracetamol
  2. Step 2: weak opioids such as codeine, dihydrocodeine, or tramadol, with or without adjuvants
  3. Step 3: strong opioids such as morphine, oxycodone, methadone, buprenorphine, or fentanyl, with a non-opioid and with or without adjuvants

The lecture presents this ladder for cancer patients and notes that it can also be used in other chronic illnesses.

Lock It In

  • Core concept: paracetamol treats pain and fever without meaningful anti-inflammatory or platelet effects.
  • Key differentiator: ketorolac is an NSAID but is used only as an analgesic.
  • Key sequence: overdose → safer pathways saturate → NAPQI accumulates → glutathione falls → liver damage.
  • Exam cue: N-acetylcysteine is the antidote for paracetamol toxicity.
Acute inflammatory arthritis

Gout pathogenesis and control of the acute flare

Acute gout is an inflammatory response to monosodium urate crystals. The immediate goal is to interrupt inflammation, not to lower urate during the attack.

What gout is

  • Metabolic disease: recurrent episodes of acute arthritis caused by monosodium urate deposits in joints and cartilage
  • Possible associated findings: uric acid renal calculi, tophi, and interstitial nephritis
  • Hyperuricemia: serum uric acid above 6.8 mg per dL
  • Important nuance: most patients with hyperuricemia never develop clinical gout. The lecture states that asymptomatic hyperuricemia has no proven benefit from treatment.
p. 7

Pathologic cascade

1. Urate crystalsDetected by the NLRP3 protein complex.
2. Inflammasome activationProstaglandins and IL-1 are released.
3. Neutrophil recruitmentPMN leukocytes move into the joint space by diapedesis.
4. AmplificationInflammation increases. Later macrophages ingest crystals and release more prostaglandins.

What this flow means: the gout flare is a self-amplifying inflammatory cascade. This is why effective acute drugs target prostaglandins, leukocyte movement, microtubules, glucocorticoid-responsive inflammatory pathways, or IL-1. p. 7

Therapeutic phases of gout
PhaseDrug groups listedMain purpose
Acute goutNSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoidsRapid relief of inflammation and pain
Intercritical goutNSAIDs, colchicineProphylaxis between attacks, especially when urate-lowering therapy is started
Chronic goutAllopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid, pegloticaseReduce urate burden and prevent recurrence or complications

NSAIDs for acute gout

  • Common choices: ibuprofen, indomethacin, and naproxen
  • Mechanism in the lecture: inhibit phagocytosis of urate crystals and inhibit prostaglandin synthesis
  • Exceptions: aspirin, salicylates, and tolmetin
  • Aspirin trap: analgesic-range doses retain uric acid
  • Adverse-effect domains: GI, cardiovascular, and renal
p. 7

Colchicine

  • Main mechanism: binds tubulin and prevents microtubule polymerization, reducing leukocyte migration and phagocytosis
  • Inflammasome effect: disrupts NLRP3-related caspase-1 activation and lowers IL-1β and IL-18
  • Timing: initiate within 24 hours and not later than 36 hours in the lecture
  • Acute dose: 1 mg followed by 500 micrograms one hour later
  • Effect: relieves gout pain and inflammation within 12 to 24 hours without changing urate metabolism or excretion
  • Common toxicity: diarrhea
  • Caution: hepatic or renal impairment and CYP3A4 inhibitors
p. 7

Glucocorticoids

  • Mechanism: reduce activation, proliferation, and survival of inflammatory cells, reduce neutrophil migration, and inhibit prostaglandins and proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β
  • Role: not first line, but a useful alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated
  • Renal disease: presented as a better alternative than NSAIDs in renal impairment or chronic kidney disease
  • Tapering: important because abrupt withdrawal may cause adrenal insufficiency
  • Joint infection: rule out before intra-articular administration
pp. 7–8

IL-1 inhibitors in acute gout

  • Agents: anakinra, canakinumab, and rilonacept
  • Rationale: IL-1β is the main proinflammatory cytokine emphasized in gout
  • Status: not FDA approved for acute gout in the lecture
  • Conditional use: reserved for contraindication or refractory disease
  • Last resort: the lecture explicitly places them after traditional therapies
p. 8

Lock It In

  • Core concept: acute gout treatment suppresses inflammation rather than lowering urate.
  • Key differentiator: colchicine blocks microtubules and leukocyte migration.
  • Key sequence: crystals → NLRP3 → IL-1 and prostaglandins → neutrophils → flare.
  • Exam cue: aspirin is not an analgesic choice for gout.
Urate-lowering therapy

Chronic and refractory gout

Chronic treatment lowers the total urate burden. The main distinction is whether the drug reduces production, increases excretion, or converts uric acid into a more easily eliminated product.

Targets and initiation

  • Serum urate target: below 6 mg per dL. The lecture gives below 5 mg per dL for tophaceous gout during allopurinol initiation.
  • First-line drugs: allopurinol and febuxostat
  • Flare prophylaxis: NSAID or colchicine for 3 to 6 months when urate-lowering therapy begins
  • Strong indication in the cited 2020 ACR guidance: tophi, radiographic gout damage, or at least two attacks per year
p. 8

Allopurinol

  • Class: purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor
  • Role: the most important urate-lowering drug in chronic gout in the lecture
  • Mechanism: purine analogue that inhibits xanthine oxidase, lowering formation of uric acid and overall urate burden
  • Active metabolite: alloxanthine or oxypurinol also inhibits xanthine oxidase and has a half-life of about 15 hours
  • Dosing: usually once daily. Start at 100 mg per day and titrate. In CKD, the lecture starts at 50 mg per day.
  • During a flare: do not stop an established allopurinol regimen because stopping may worsen recovery.
p. 8

Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome

  • Presentation: Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, eosinophilia, leukocytosis, fever, hepatitis, and renal failure
  • Timing: often within 2 to 4 weeks after starting therapy
  • Action: stop at the first sign of rash
  • Risk factors: high starting dose, renal dysfunction, diuretics, amoxicillin, ampicillin, and HLA-B*5801
  • Screening: recommended in the lecture for Han Chinese, Korean, or Thai descent. Avoid allopurinol with a positive test.

Allopurinol interactions

  • Azathioprine: increased concentration and fatal cytopenia risk. The lecture says concomitant use requires major dose reduction.
  • Cyclophosphamide concentration may increase.
  • Warfarin and other oral anticoagulants may increase.
  • Hepatic iron concentration may increase.
p. 8
Chronic gout drugs
DrugMechanismWhen it fitsMajor caution
FebuxostatPotent selective non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitorFirst-line alternative when allopurinol is not tolerated or ineffective. Appears safe in moderate kidney disease in the lecture.Black-box warning for cardiovascular death. Liver test abnormalities, diarrhea, headache, and nausea may occur.
ProbenecidInhibits proximal tubular transport, decreasing net uric acid reabsorption and increasing uricosuriaUnderexcretion of uric acid when xanthine oxidase inhibition is contraindicated, or with tophi. May be used alone or with an XO inhibitor.Renal stones. Increase oral fluids. Avoid with high uric acid excretion, renal calculi, or stage above 3 CKD in the lecture.

Pegloticase details

  • Dose: 8 mg IV every 2 weeks
  • Effect: rapid action with peak effect in 24 to 72 hours. A single infusion lowers urate for up to 21 days in the lecture.
  • Methotrexate combination: increases efficacy and decreases many allergic reactions
  • Other adverse effects: gout flare, nephrolithiasis, arthralgia, muscle spasm, headache, anemia, nausea, upper respiratory infection, urinary tract infection, edema, and diarrhea
p. 9

Lock It In

  • Core concept: chronic gout therapy lowers the urate burden.
  • Key differentiator: allopurinol and febuxostat reduce production. Probenecid increases excretion. Pegloticase converts uric acid to allantoin.
  • Key sequence: start ULT → temporary flare risk → give NSAID or colchicine prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months.
  • Exam cue: febuxostat carries a cardiovascular death warning.
Disease modification

Rheumatoid arthritis and the DMARD framework

Rheumatoid arthritis is a progressive immunologic disease. The goal is not only symptom relief, but arrest or slowing of the tissue-damaging process.

Why DMARDs matter

  • Rheumatoid arthritis: progressive immunologic disease with systemic effects, reduced mobility, reduced quality of life, and shortened life
  • Primary goal: arrest or slow progression by modifying the disease itself
  • Time to effect: 2 weeks to 6 months may be required for clinical benefit
  • Unique role: DMARDs achieve symptom relief and disease modification. NSAIDs do not alter the course of arthritic disease.
p. 9
Major DMARD families
FamilyExamples in the lectureOrganizing idea
Conventional synthetic DMARDsMethotrexate, leflunomide, azathioprine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, cyclophosphamide, calcineurin inhibitors, mycophenolate, mesalamine, sulfasalazineOlder small molecules with diverse intracellular and metabolic targets
Targeted synthetic DMARDsBaricitinib, tofacitinib, upadacitinib, apremilastSmall molecules directed at JAK signaling or PDE4
Biologic DMARDsAbatacept, rituximab, IL-1 inhibitors, IL-6 inhibitors, TNF-α inhibitors, and other cytokine-directed agentsProteins or antibodies directed at cells, receptors, or cytokines
BiosimilarsVersions of rituximab, adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximabVery similar efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity with potential lower cost

Shared toxicity logic

Many DMARD adverse effects follow from immune suppression or tissue toxicity. Across the lecture, repeatedly watch for infection, cytopenias, liver injury, GI effects, organ-specific toxicity, and malignancy. The exact pattern depends on the target and drug.

Lock It In

  • Core concept: DMARDs modify the disease process.
  • Key differentiator: synthetic agents are small molecules. Biologics are larger targeted proteins or antibodies.
  • Key sequence: immune target inhibition → reduced inflammatory-cell signaling or proliferation → slower tissue damage.
  • Exam cue: methotrexate is the most important conventional synthetic DMARD in the lecture.
Conventional synthetic DMARDs

Methotrexate, leflunomide, azathioprine, and antimalarials

These agents differ sharply in mechanism, but the lecture repeatedly tests their signature toxicities and rescue measures.

Methotrexate

  • Mechanism: inhibits AICAR transformylase and thymidylate synthetase, raising extracellular AMP and suppressing neutrophils, dendritic cells, macrophages, and lymphocytes
  • Other effects: changes polymorphonuclear chemotaxis, inhibits proliferation, stimulates apoptosis, and has minor dihydrofolate reductase effects
  • RA benefit: decreases the appearance of new erosions
  • Routes: oral, subcutaneous, and intramuscular
  • Dose pattern: weekly, not daily
  • Common adverse effects: nausea and stomatitis
  • Other toxicity: leukopenia, anemia, GI ulceration, alopecia, and dose-related liver enzyme elevation
  • Rescue support: leucovorin or folic acid reduces stomatitis, GI effects, and liver abnormalities but may reduce efficacy
  • Contraindication: pregnancy
p. 10

Leflunomide

  • Mechanism: active metabolite A77 1726 inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase, reduces ribonucleotide synthesis, and arrests cells in G1
  • Immune effects: reduces T-cell proliferation and B-cell antibody production
  • Efficacy: equal to methotrexate in RA, including inhibition of bony erosions
  • Half-life: about 19 days because of enterohepatic recirculation
  • Cholestyramine: shortens the half-life to about one day
  • Common adverse effect: diarrhea, occurring in about 25 percent in the lecture
  • Other toxicity: liver abnormalities, mild alopecia, weight gain, increased blood pressure, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia
p. 10

Azathioprine

  • Metabolism: converted to 6-mercaptopurine, then 6-thioguanine
  • Mechanism: suppresses inosinic acid synthesis, B-cell and T-cell function, immunoglobulin production, and IL-2 secretion
  • Uses listed: active RA and prevention of kidney transplant rejection, with several other autoimmune uses
  • Major adverse effects: GI disturbance, bone marrow suppression, infection, and cancer risk
  • Genetic risk: leukopenia with NUDT15 polymorphism and TPMT homozygosity
  • Critical interaction: allopurinol can raise azathioprine levels and cause fatal cytopenia
pp. 8, 10

Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine

  • Mechanisms listed: suppress T-cell responses, inhibit leukocyte chemotaxis, stabilize lysosomal processing, inhibit DNA and RNA synthesis, and interfere with type I interferon through TLR7 and TLR9
  • Uses: primarily malaria, plus RA, SLE, discoid lupus, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and Sjögren syndrome
  • Response time: 3 to 6 months
  • Signature toxicity: retinopathy
  • Monitoring: baseline eye examination before therapy
  • Other toxicity: GI effects, rash, cytopenias, myopathy, cardiomyopathy, conduction disorders, neuromyotoxicity, and nightmares
  • Half-life: very long at 40 to 50 days
  • Pregnancy: described as relatively safe
pp. 10–11

Lock It In

  • Core concept: conventional DMARDs use different intracellular mechanisms to suppress immune-driven disease.
  • Key differentiator: methotrexate is weekly and is the central conventional drug. Leflunomide has a very long half-life.
  • Key sequence: leflunomide enterohepatic recirculation → prolonged half-life → cholestyramine accelerates removal.
  • Exam cue: hydroxychloroquine requires retinal monitoring.
Conventional synthetic DMARDs

Cytotoxic drugs, antimetabolites, aminosalicylates, and calcineurin inhibitors

This group is best remembered by linking each mechanism to a signature toxicity.

About 30 percent discontinue in the lecture. Serious effects include TEN, hemolysis, methemoglobinemia, agranulocytosis, pulmonary toxicity, lupus, and reversible male infertility.
Calcineurin inhibitorsCyclosporine and voclosporin bind cyclophilin. Tacrolimus binds FKBP. All inhibit calcineurin and T-cell cytokine transcription.Severe active RA, SLE including nephritis, psoriasis, transplant rejection, and several refractory inflammatory diseasesCYP3A4 interactions. High doses can be cardiotoxic, neurotoxic, and nephrotoxic. Grapefruit juice raises cyclosporine bioavailability in the lecture.

Cyclophosphamide mechanism-to-toxicity link

ActivationLiver CYP450 creates active metabolites.
Therapeutic metabolitePhosphoramide mustard crosslinks DNA.
Toxic metaboliteAcrolein injures the bladder.
ProtectionHydration and mesna neutralize or reduce acrolein-related injury.
p. 11

Mesalamine versus sulfasalazine

  • Mesalamine: 5-ASA is the active moiety in inflammatory bowel disease.
  • Sulfasalazine: adds sulfapyridine, which is active in RA but causes most toxicity.
  • Do not confuse: the extra metabolite explains why sulfasalazine has an RA indication and more troublesome adverse effects.
p. 11

Lock It In

  • Core concept: signature toxicities often reveal the drug.
  • Key differentiator: mycophenolate is used in several autoimmune diseases but is not proven effective in RA.
  • Key sequence: cyclophosphamide → phosphoramide mustard for benefit and acrolein for bladder injury.
  • Exam cue: mesna protects against cyclophosphamide-associated hemorrhagic cystitis.
Targeted synthetic DMARDs

JAK inhibitors and apremilast

These are orally active small molecules aimed at defined signaling pathways. Their major warnings are as important as their mechanisms.

Janus kinase inhibitors

Baricitinib, tofacitinib, and upadacitinib interrupt JAK-STAT signaling. This pathway has a major role in autoimmune disease such as rheumatoid arthritis. pp. 11–12

DrugSelectivity or metabolismPractical lecture point
BaricitinibJAK1 and JAK3 greater than JAK2 in the lecture. Not metabolized by CYP3A4.Fewer CYP3A4 interactions.
TofacitinibInhibits all listed JAK members. About 70 percent CYP3A4 metabolism.Dose reduction with liver impairment or CYP inhibitors.
UpadacitinibJAK1 and JAK2 greater than JAK3. Highly protein bound.Poorly cleared by dialysis and requires caution in renal impairment.

Shared adverse effects

  • Infections: upper respiratory infections and herpes zoster
  • Laboratory changes: increased liver tests, total cholesterol, and LDL
  • Rare effects: lymphoma, neutropenia, lymphopenia, anemia, and GI perforation with diverticulitis history
  • Black-box warning: venous thromboembolism, DVT, pulmonary embolism, major adverse cardiovascular events, and cancer
  • Use: all may treat RA with poor response to TNF-α inhibitors

Apremilast

  • Class: phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor
  • Mechanism: prevents conversion of cAMP to AMP, raising intracellular cAMP and reducing proinflammatory cytokines listed in the lecture
  • Uses: plaque psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and oral ulcers associated with Behçet disease
  • Common adverse effects: diarrhea and nausea
  • Other concerns: abdominal pain, vomiting, upper respiratory infections, arthralgia, weight loss, headache, mood disorders, and suicidal ideation
  • Pharmacokinetics: 73 percent bioavailability, half-life 6 to 9 hours, about 70 percent CYP3A4 metabolism, and renal dose adjustment when creatinine clearance is below 30
p. 12

Lock It In

  • Core concept: targeted synthetic DMARDs are small molecules with defined signaling targets.
  • Key differentiator: JAK inhibitors carry major thrombotic, cardiovascular, and cancer warnings.
  • Key sequence: PDE4 inhibition → higher cAMP → lower proinflammatory cytokine production.
  • Exam cue: apremilast is associated with GI effects, weight loss, and mood concerns.
Biologic DMARDs

Cell targets, cytokines, TNF-α inhibitors, and biosimilars

Biologics suppress defined immune signals. The recurring clinical issue is infection risk, with drug-specific infusion reactions and target-specific warnings.

Abatacept

  • Structure: CTLA-4 extracellular domain fused to human IgG1 Fc
  • Mechanism: binds CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells and blocks interaction with CD28 on T cells
  • Result: inhibits T-cell activation
  • Uses: RA, psoriatic arthritis, polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis, and graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis
  • Adverse effects: infections, headache, nasopharyngitis, nausea, lymphoma risk, infusion reactions, hypersensitivity, and anaphylaxis
  • Vaccines: avoid live vaccines for up to 3 months after discontinuation
p. 12

Rituximab

  • Target: CD20-positive B lymphocytes
  • Mechanism: cell-mediated and complement-dependent cytotoxicity plus apoptosis
  • Result: rapid depletion of peripheral and synovial B cells, reducing antigen presentation and proinflammatory cytokines
  • RA use: combined with methotrexate
  • Adverse effects: rash, infusion reactions, urticaria, anaphylaxis, SJS, and serious infections
  • Hepatitis B: reactivation requires treatment or prolonged monitoring
p. 12
Cytokine inhibitors
TargetAgentsMechanism and high-yield points
IL-6 receptorTocilizumab, sarilumabBind soluble and membrane IL-6 receptors. Used in RA. Common effects include infection, increased liver enzymes, and increased LDL.
IL-1Anakinra, canakinumab, rilonaceptAnakinra blocks IL-1α and IL-1β receptor effects. Canakinumab complexes with IL-1β. Rilonacept neutralizes IL-1β. Used mainly for cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes and off-label acute gout, with limited RA use.
IL-23 or IL-12 and IL-23Guselkumab, risankizumab, ustekinumabUsed mainly for psoriasis. Ustekinumab also inhibits IL-12 and has IBD indications.
IL-17AIxekizumab, secukinumabUsed mainly for psoriasis. Secukinumab also has axial spondyloarthritis uses in the lecture.
Type I interferon or BLySAnifrolumab, belimumabPresented in the lecture as SLE-directed agents. Anifrolumab is anti-type I interferon. Belimumab is anti-BLyS.

TNF-α inhibitor identities

  • Adalimumab and golimumab: human monoclonal antibodies
  • Infliximab: chimeric monoclonal antibody with 25 percent mouse component
  • Etanercept: fusion protein containing two p75 receptors linked to human IgG Fc
  • Certolizumab: humanized Fab fragment conjugated to PEG and lacking an Fc region
  • Pregnancy point: certolizumab does not cross into breast milk or placenta in the lecture and is presented as the TNF inhibitor of choice in pregnancy

TNF-α inhibitor safety pattern

  • Common: injection-site reactions and infections
  • Severe infection: fungal infection and reactivation of hepatitis B or tuberculosis
  • Lower TB-reactivation risk: etanercept in the lecture
  • Other serious effects: worsening heart failure, demyelinating disease, lupus-like syndrome, GI problems, headache, rash, and blood dyscrasias
  • Methotrexate combination: increases efficacy and reduces anti-drug antibody formation, especially with infliximab
p. 13

Biosimilars

Biosimilars are biologic medicines designed to be highly similar to existing biologics. The lecture lists biosimilars for rituximab, adalimumab, etanercept, and infliximab. They may reduce cost and improve access, with similar efficacy, toxicity, and immunogenicity to legacy compounds. p. 13

Lock It In

  • Core concept: biologics target immune cells, receptors, or cytokines.
  • Key differentiator: abatacept blocks T-cell costimulation. Rituximab depletes CD20 B cells.
  • Key sequence: TNF block → reduced macrophage and T-cell inflammatory function → better control, but increased infection risk.
  • Exam cue: certolizumab lacks an Fc region.
Treatment strategy

Combination therapy and glucocorticoids in rheumatoid arthritis

When monotherapy is inadequate, the lecture favors rational combinations while keeping long-term glucocorticoid exposure as low as possible.

Combination therapy

  • When: moderate or high RA activity that remains refractory to DMARD monotherapy
  • Options: combinations of traditional DMARDs, addition of TNF inhibitors, non-TNF biologics, or small molecules
  • Rule: combine when monotherapy does not produce an adequate response
  • Rationale: increased efficacy may outweigh toxicity risk
  • Design principles: complementary mechanisms, non-overlapping pharmacokinetics, and non-overlapping adverse effects
  • Anchor drug: many agents show improved efficacy when added to methotrexate
p. 14

Glucocorticoids in RA

  • Effect: potent, prompt, and dramatic anti-inflammatory action
  • Disease effect: capable of slowing new bone erosions
  • Extra-articular use: pericarditis or eye involvement
  • Long-term prednisone: should not exceed 7.5 mg daily in the lecture
  • Goal: gradual reduction and eventual discontinuation when possible
  • Major concern: chronic use causes devastating adverse effects and raises infection risk
  • Even low dose: 2.8 mg per day for more than 5 years is associated with severe infection in the lecture
p. 14

Rational combination checklist

Mechanisms

Choose complementary targets rather than redundant ones.

Pharmacokinetics

Avoid combinations with problematic overlapping disposition.

Adverse effects

Prefer non-overlapping toxicity patterns.

Response

Escalate because disease remains active, not simply because more drugs are available.

Lock It In

  • Core concept: combination therapy is for inadequate response to monotherapy.
  • Key differentiator: methotrexate is the most common combination anchor in this lecture.
  • Key sequence: persistent disease activity → rational combination → greater efficacy with controlled toxicity.
  • Exam cue: long-term prednisone should be minimized and gradually reduced.
Final rapid review

Cram Sheet

Use this tab for retrieval. Every item below has already been explained in the lesson.

NSAID essentials

  • Chief mechanism: inhibit prostanoid biosynthesis through COX inhibition
  • COX-1: housekeeping, gastric protection, platelet thromboxane
  • COX-2: inflammation, endothelial prostacyclin, renal development
  • Four effects: analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antipyretic, and usually antiplatelet
  • Rule: lowest effective dose for the shortest duration
  • All weak acids except: nabumetone
  • All reversible except: aspirin

NSAID traps

  • Selective COX-2: lower GI irritation but no cardioprotection
  • Aspirin in children with viral illness: Reye syndrome
  • Aspirin in gout: uric acid retention at analgesic doses
  • Ketorolac: analgesia only, nephrotoxic, no more than 5 days
  • Pregnancy: avoid from 20 weeks for low amniotic fluid and from 30 weeks for ductus closure
  • Black-box domains: cardiovascular thrombosis and GI bleeding

Paracetamol and tramadol

  • Paracetamol: pain and fever without significant anti-inflammatory or platelet effects
  • Overdose: NAPQI accumulation and glutathione depletion
  • Antidote: N-acetylcysteine
  • Major toxicity: liver injury
  • Tramadol: weak μ-opioid action plus serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibition
  • Tramadol concerns: serotonin syndrome and seizures

Acute gout

  • Hyperuricemia: above 6.8 mg per dL
  • Pathway: urate crystals → NLRP3 → IL-1 and prostaglandins → neutrophils
  • Acute drugs: NSAIDs, colchicine, glucocorticoids
  • Colchicine: blocks tubulin polymerization and leukocyte migration
  • Common colchicine toxicity: diarrhea
  • IL-1 inhibitors: last-resort options in refractory or contraindicated cases

Chronic gout

  • Target: serum urate below 6 mg per dL
  • Allopurinol: purine XO inhibitor and first-line chronic drug
  • Allopurinol danger: AHS, SJS, and TEN. Stop at rash.
  • Febuxostat: non-purine XO inhibitor with CV death warning
  • Probenecid: uricosuric and stone risk
  • Pegloticase: converts uric acid to allantoin. Avoid in G6PD deficiency.
  • Initiation: add NSAID or colchicine prophylaxis for 3 to 6 months

Signature DMARD toxicities

  • Methotrexate: nausea, stomatitis, cytopenias, liver injury. Leucovorin or folate support.
  • Leflunomide: diarrhea and liver effects. Cholestyramine accelerates elimination.
  • Hydroxychloroquine: retinopathy
  • Cyclophosphamide: hemorrhagic cystitis. Mesna protects.
  • JAK inhibitors: VTE, DVT, PE, MACE, and cancer warning
  • Biologics: injection or infusion reactions, infection, and lymphoma risk
  • TNF inhibitors: severe infection, TB or HBV reactivation, CHF, demyelination, and lupus-like syndrome

Final exception list

  1. Nabumetone is the non-acid NSAID.
  2. Aspirin is the irreversible NSAID.
  3. Selective COX-2 inhibitors and non-acetylated salicylates do not inhibit platelet aggregation.
  4. Aspirin, salicylates, and tolmetin are acute gout exceptions.
  5. DMARDs, not NSAIDs, slow the rheumatic disease process.
  6. Indomethacin and ibuprofen can close PDA in preterm infants.
  7. Certolizumab lacks an Fc region.
